opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that post-training has a few different jobs, and RL is increasingly the one doing the heavy lifting for the parts that matter most right now.

If you go back a couple of years, the standard picture was: you pre-train a big base model, then you do supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations to get it to follow instructions and adopt a certain format and persona, and then you do some RLHF on top to polish it, to make it more helpful, less likely to say weird things, more aligned with what people prefer. In that picture RL was kind of the last-mile thing. It was about style and preferences, and a lot of people were skeptical about whether it was teaching the model anything new or just reshaping what was already there.

What's changed is that we've found RL is really good at eliciting and sharpening capabilities when you have a signal you can verify. Math problems where you can check the answer, code where you can run the tests, tasks in an environment where you can tell whether the agent actually accomplished the goal. When you have that kind of reward, you can let the model try things, think for a long time, explore different strategies, and reinforce what actually works. That's where you get the reasoning behaviors, the backtracking, the self-checking, and it's not something you can easily get just by imitating demonstrations, because the model is learning from its own attempts rather than copying someone else's.

So I think of SFT as getting the model into the right neighborhood: teaching it the format, the tools, the basic shape of the task. Then RL is where it gets good, where it learns to actually solve the problem robustly in its own way. And then there's still a layer of preference tuning and safety work on top for deployment, because you care about things that aren't easy to verify, like tone, honesty, and when to refuse.

The bigger shift, I'd say, is that RL is moving from something a handful of labs do at the very end to something much more central and much more about environments. The question becomes: what are the tasks, what are the tools, how do you grade success? Designing good environments and good rewards is turning into a core part of building a model for a real use case, and I think that's going to be true not just for frontier labs but for anyone who wants a model that's really good at a specific thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says RL is increasingly doing the “heavy lifting,” but does not state that it consumes most post-training compute.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes SFT, RL, and preference and safety tuning as parts of post-training that prepare a model for deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that pretraining gives you this enormous prior over everything humans have written, and post-training is the process of shaping that into something that actually behaves the way you want when someone's sitting in front of it. And RL is really the last mile of that, but it's increasingly the most important mile.

If you break post-training down, you've got supervised fine-tuning, which is essentially showing the model examples of the format and style you want. That's very sample-efficient, it's cheap, but it's fundamentally imitation. The model can only get as good as the demonstrations you give it. Then you've got preference-based methods like DPO or RLHF with a reward model, which are about nudging the model toward outputs people like over outputs they don't. That's great for things like tone, helpfulness, safety, the stuff that's hard to specify but easy to recognize.

And then what's changed in the last couple of years is RL with verifiable rewards. Math, code, anything where you can actually check whether the answer is right. And that's a qualitatively different thing, because now the model isn't bounded by the demonstrations anymore. It can discover strategies, it can learn to think for longer, backtrack, verify its own work, and those behaviors emerge because they're rewarded, not because someone wrote them down.

So the role of RL in the broader pipeline, to me, is that it's the part where the model stops copying and starts optimizing. SFT gets it into the right neighborhood, preference tuning makes it pleasant and safe to interact with, and RL is where you actually push capability. And the frontier right now is really about expanding what counts as a verifiable environment. Agentic tasks, tool use, multi-turn stuff, things where the reward signal is noisier or delayed. That's where I think most of the interesting work is, because the algorithms are honestly not that complicated. GRPO is a few lines of math. The hard part is building environments that are rich enough to teach the model something real and robust enough that it can't just game them.

r001.rationale: The response calls RL the “last mile” and “increasingly the most important mile,” but does not state that it consumes most of the post-training compute.

r002.rationale: It describes post-training as shaping the pretrained model for deployment and identifies RL alongside supervised fine-tuning and preference-based methods as parts of that process.

astra-6.text:
I think of post-training as taking the capabilities a model acquired during pretraining and turning them into behavior that’s useful in a particular setting. The model may know a lot, but that doesn’t automatically mean it knows when to use a tool, when to ask a clarifying question, or how much effort to spend on a problem.

Supervised fine-tuning gives you a way to demonstrate that behavior: here’s what a good response looks like. Reinforcement learning lets you go a step further and say, here’s what we’re trying to accomplish—try different approaches, get feedback, and become more likely to do the things that work. That’s especially valuable when it’s easier to judge an outcome than to write down the ideal sequence of steps to reach it.

But the feedback is really the central thing. You’re optimizing against some measurable signal, and that signal is never a complete description of what you want in deployment. So I see RL as one component of a larger loop: define the task, build good feedback, train, evaluate the resulting behavior, and use what you learn to improve the setup. It’s powerful, but it doesn’t replace the work of deciding what good behavior actually means.

r001.rationale: The response discusses RL’s value and feedback but does not state that it consumes most post-training compute for large-scale models.

r002.rationale: It describes post-training as shaping pretrained capabilities into useful behavior for deployment and explicitly calls RL one component of a larger loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as one part of post-training, where you take a pretrained model that has a broad set of capabilities and try to turn it into something useful in a particular setting. Pretraining gives you a starting point, but it doesn’t necessarily give you the behavior you want when you put the model in front of a user.

Typically, you’ll use supervised fine-tuning to show the model examples of good behavior, and then reinforcement learning lets you optimize against feedback on what it actually produces. That feedback might be human preferences, or it might be something you can check automatically, like whether a piece of code passes tests.

The interesting thing is that you’re specifying what makes an outcome good without necessarily specifying every step the model should take to get there. That gives it room to discover better strategies. But the objective matters enormously: improving the reward isn’t automatically the same thing as making the model better for deployment. So I see RL as part of a larger loop of training, evaluation, and understanding where the model still fails.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that reinforcement learning often consumes most of the post-training compute for large-scale models.

r002.rationale: It describes reinforcement learning as one part of post-training that adapts a pretrained model toward useful behavior in a particular setting.
